title: Editing the Atlas weekly requires only a Governance Poll while changing the Protocol requires a Poll and an Executive Vote
content:
A.1.11.1.3.0.3.2 records why the Weekly Governance Cycle was divided: with the introduction of the Atlas Edit Weekly Cycle, the old undifferentiated cycle had to split into two subtypes that "differ in terms of the permissioned parties authorized to trigger a proposal and the governance mechanisms involved."

The mechanism difference is stark. "The Atlas Edit Weekly Cycle implements edits to the Atlas via the mechanism of a Governance Poll only," and A.1.11.2.2 confirms that "successful polls trigger direct edits to the Atlas." The Operational Weekly Cycle, by contrast, "can action changes to the Protocol that require Atlas edits, and generally requires both a Governance Poll and an Executive Vote."

That produces a counterintuitive asymmetry: amending the constitutional text is procedurally *lighter* than adjusting a live parameter. The Atlas can be rewritten on a three-day non-binding Poll, while a debt-ceiling change needs the same Poll plus a bundled, reviewed, delay-gated on-chain Executive.

The justification is that the two acts differ in immediacy of consequence — an Atlas edit changes what future actors are obliged to do, whereas an Executive Vote moves funds and risk now. But the asymmetry has a real cost: the document that authorizes everything else is the cheapest artifact in the system to change, and the compensating controls sit entirely in the delegate stake and the Core Facilitator's misalignment veto rather than in the vote itself.
description: The Weekly Cycle was split into an Atlas Edit subtype and an Operational subtype, differing in who may trigger proposals and in how many votes they must clear.
